990.bp: When you ask a search engine or recommendation system to rank items, that system has learned from real-world data. But real-world data carries human biases—maybe certain groups are shown less often, or treated worse. We want ranking systems to work fairly for everyone, not amplify hidden societal patterns already baked into the data.
990.wh: Existing fairness solutions typically ask you to know which attributes matter (gender, race, age) and label them in your training data. This is hard in practice—sensitive data is often private, expensive to label, or legally risky to even collect. You need a way to detect and fix bias without needing these explicit labels.
990.po: On a real search benchmark (MS MARCO), their method reduced gender bias without needing demographic labels, and the ranking quality stayed the same or got better compared to other approaches. The fix was built into the learning process itself, not bolted on afterward.
990.ww: The core insight is that a model's loss (how wrong it is on each example) can tell you about bias. When the model makes confidently wrong predictions on items from one demographic group, that's often a sign of bias. By training in stages—first getting good at easy examples, then hard ones—the system learns to weigh examples fairly and doesn't overfit to biased patterns in the data.
990.ap: The method starts training on examples the model finds easiest (lowest loss). As it improves, it gradually adds harder examples into the training mix. Throughout, it watches whether the prediction errors differ between demographic groups, even though it never actually sees group labels. The size and pattern of those errors serve as a proxy for bias, letting the learning process self-correct.

991.bp: In real systems, measurements change over time and depend on each other—like network traffic, stock prices, or sensor readings in a factory. To make better decisions, we need to know which measurements actually cause changes in others, not just which ones tend to move together. This is especially hard when there are hidden factors influencing everything.
991.wh: Real-world time series have confounders—unobserved forces that affect multiple variables at once. For example, a holiday might boost both website traffic and product orders, but the holiday itself isn't measured in your data. Standard causal discovery methods assume you measure everything important, which breaks down when confounders hide.
991.po: The framework handles real time series data with hidden confounders and captures how causal relationships shift over time, enabling better interpretation and decision-making in domains like finance, operations, and healthcare where the ground truth often changes.
991.ww: By modeling confounders at multiple scales (some steady over time, some shifting moment-to-moment), the system can explain away the effects of hidden variables and reveal the true direct relationships between the things you do measure. This works because hidden influences have characteristic patterns—persistent ones show up the same way at every time step, while transient ones don't.
991.ap: The method builds two kinds of causal graphs in parallel. Coarse-grained graphs capture relationships across entire sequences (does variable A always lead to variable B?), while fine-grained graphs zoom in to local time windows (does the relationship change here?). A separate neural network specifically designed to find proxies for unobserved confounders sits alongside, detecting which hidden factors are at play and adjusting the causal conclusions accordingly.

992.bp: Recommendation systems often rely on knowledge bases—structured facts like movie genres, actor relationships, or product properties. These knowledge bases help systems recommend things intelligently. But real-world knowledge bases are messy: facts are missing (incomplete), some facts are wrong (noisy), and this mess directly damages the quality of recommendations.
992.wh: Most recommendation systems focus on building clever models to extract value from messy data as-is. But if the data itself is full of errors and gaps, even the cleverest model can't fix that. You need a way to clean up and fill in the knowledge base itself, not just tolerate its messiness.
992.po: The method treats knowledge base quality as a data problem, not a model problem. By generating high-quality facts to fill gaps and removing noisy ones, the system improves recommendation performance without requiring manual annotation or domain expertise, working on real knowledge graphs used in production systems.
992.ww: Diffusion models are trained to gradually turn pure noise into realistic data by learning the true patterns in data. The insight here is that a knowledge base is just data—so a diffusion model can learn the true patterns of what correct, complete knowledge looks like, then convert a messy real knowledge base into a clean synthetic one that preserves the original structure but fixes quality issues.
992.ap: The method trains a special diffusion model that learns the actual distribution of knowledge graphs (which facts tend to go together, which entities relate to which). This model is shaped to care most about facts that matter for recommendations. Once trained, it can take the real, messy knowledge base and gradually refine it, removing noise and inferring missing facts until it produces a high-quality version suitable for downstream recommendations.

993.bp: Information retrieval—search, ranking, answering questions—sits at the intersection of technology and power. These systems decide what information billions of people see, who gets found in searches, and whose voice reaches whom. Today, they're increasingly sites of conflict between helping people access truth and oppressing them through manipulation and surveillance.
993.wh: Current fairness and transparency approaches focus on algorithmic metrics—bias numbers, attention weights—but miss the bigger political question: whose interests does the system serve? In an era of democratic erosion and tech concentration, a well-calibrated bias number doesn't prevent a system from being weaponized for oppression or surveillance.
993.po: This is a call for the research community to take seriously the political and social dimensions of information retrieval, to build critical theories and practices into the field, and to recognize that the technical and the political are inseparable.
993.ww: The argument is that information access is not a neutral technical problem. Who controls search engines and what they choose to rank shapes society. Systems can be simultaneously 'fair' by metrics and deeply unjust in practice. Real emancipatory work requires understanding power structures and centering the experiences of marginalized communities in system design.
993.ap: Rather than proposing a technical solution, this positions information retrieval as a political practice that must engage with critical theory—asking not just 'is this ranking fair?' but 'fair to whom, and toward what end?' It challenges researchers to design systems explicitly with emancipatory goals and to resist surveillance and authoritarian capture of information infrastructure.

994.bp: People ask questions expecting useful, appropriate answers tailored to who they are and what they need. Over decades, researchers built systems that understood questions, found relevant information, and generated coherent responses. Now large language models can generate fluent text, but old questions remain: how do we know an answer fits the person asking it? How do we balance accuracy with understandability?
994.wh: The jump from document retrieval to generative AI feels like a clean break, but it leaves unsolved problems behind. Large language models are powerful but opaque, and user modeling—understanding what each individual actually needs—is harder than ever. How do you ensure an LLM-generated answer is right for a particular person, not just plausible-sounding?
994.po: The paper bridges historical work in user modeling and natural language generation with modern large language models, showing that old insights about personalization, clarity, and coherence still matter even when the underlying technology has changed completely.
994.ww: The core insight is that generating any old answer isn't enough. Good answers depend on two things: the information need (what are they really asking for) and the user (who are they, what do they know, what can they understand). This was true fifty years ago with symbolic systems and remains true today with LLMs.
994.ap: The talk surveys the history of how question-answering systems handled these two dimensions—understanding information needs through sophisticated dialogue, and tailoring answers to the audience (complexity, terminology, depth). It positions modern large language models as tools for these old problems, not replacements for thinking about them.

995.bp: For two decades, search meant finding and ranking documents. Today it's shifting: instead of returning documents, we want systems that can read evidence, think through a problem, and actually do things—book flights, analyze data, plan projects. This changes what retrieval means and creates new technical challenges.
995.wh: When you have a reasoning system connected to the internet, it's not obvious what should trigger retrieval (when to stop reasoning and look something up), what information matters most, or how to evaluate whether the system worked. These questions barely existed when search just meant ranking documents.
995.po: Real systems like Search-o1 and DeepAgent demonstrate that modern language models can chain reasoning with active search—they know when their knowledge ends and go fetch what they need. This creates qualitatively new capabilities: deep research over many steps, tool use at scale, and systems that actually execute information-seeking goals.
995.ww: The mechanism is that large reasoning models can explain their reasoning transparently (here's what I know, here's what I'm unsure about, here's what I should search for). By giving them access to retrieval, they can interrupt their reasoning to look things up, then resume. This is much more flexible than the old pipeline where retrieval came first and reasoning second.
995.ap: Systems like FlashRAG provide modular platforms where the reasoning model and the retriever collaborate. The reasoning model decides when and what to search for, the retrieval system finds relevant information, and the model integrates it. The hardest new problems are tracking what's been retrieved (maintaining memory), checking whether retrieved information is accurate, and evaluating whether a multi-step reasoning-and-retrieval process actually solved the problem.

996.bp: People search differently depending on who they are—age, language skill, cultural background, and the task at hand all shape how someone formulates queries and interacts with results. If a search engine is designed for one type of searcher, it won't work well for others. Understanding these differences helps build fairer, more robust systems.
996.wh: Most search systems are evaluated on average performance across all users, which can mask failures for specific groups. If a system works great for one demographic but poorly for another, traditional benchmarks won't catch it. You need to understand the underlying patterns in how different people search differently.
996.po: Through controlled user studies, the work shows that age is the strongest predictor of search behavior—older users formulate queries differently and navigate results differently than younger users. Gender and language effects exist but are more selective. Most importantly, these differences reflect strategy choices, not inability—they're variations in how people approach the task.
996.ww: Instead of assuming everyone searches the same way, the insight is that people pick different strategies based on their experience and comfort level. Younger users might prefer shorter queries and quick scanning, while older users might structure queries more carefully. Neither is worse; they're just different. Understanding this helps systems adapt to each person rather than punishing anyone whose style differs from the norm.
996.ap: Researchers had participants of different ages, genders, and language abilities perform search tasks and recorded their query formulation, click patterns, and session behavior. They extracted simple underlying 'dimensions' that capture the variation (like how structured vs. exploratory someone's search strategy is), and showed these dimensions explain observed behavior better than just saying 'age groups are different.'

997.bp: Recommendation systems work by learning what items are similar to each other. But similarity in the real world isn't just structural—it's emotional. You might want music that sounds happy even if it's orchestrated totally differently, or books with similar themes even if they're in different genres. Baking emotion into how systems measure similarity improves what they recommend.
997.wh: Graph-based recommendation systems treat items as nodes and similarity as edges. But two items can be structurally adjacent (nearby in the graph) while being emotionally different (one uplifting, one depressing). When the system propagates information along edges, it mixes signals from items that shouldn't influence each other, degrading recommendation quality.
997.po: The system improved top-K recommendation accuracy across multiple music, book, and media datasets while actually reducing computational cost compared to baseline methods. This shows that emotional alignment is not just nice-to-have but actively improves practical recommendation performance.
997.ww: Human-centered preference isn't just facts—it's feelings. When you model items using only their structural relationships, you miss the affective dimension. By extracting emotional properties (valence: positive vs. negative; arousal: energetic vs. calm) and ensuring the learned representations respect these emotional boundaries, the system produces recommendations that feel right, not just structurally plausible.
997.ap: The method encodes emotional dimensions (extracted from language models) as a topological structure that represents the affective space. As the system learns to rank items, it adds a loss function that rewards embeddings aligned with this affective structure. This gently steers learned representations toward emotional consistency: items close in the learned space are not just structurally similar but also affectively similar.

998.bp: Search engines are adding generative summaries (AI Overviews) directly at the top of results, before the traditional ranked links. This is a major interface change. We need to understand how this affects user behavior—do people still read the traditional results, or do they stop at the summary? Does this help or harm how people search?
998.wh: When you change the layout of a search result page dramatically, users might navigate differently than before. The question isn't just whether they like the new feature—it's whether it changes fundamental search behavior in ways that could be harmful (less exploration, higher dependency on summaries) or beneficial (faster answers, less reading required).
998.po: Eye-tracking shows that users do engage more with generative summaries than before, but they still look at traditional ranked results and follow similar patterns documented in decades of prior research. The classic "golden triangle" of attention (top-left section gets most gaze) still holds. Users are making a choice to engage with new features while maintaining existing behaviors.
998.ww: Generative summaries are attractive and prominent, so people naturally look at them first. But they're not a complete replacement—users still value the original ranked links because they offer different information (you can click through and verify, explore multiple viewpoints, judge source credibility). The system works when both coexist and users can choose which to use.
998.ap: Researchers placed eye-tracking cameras while users performed search tasks on an interface with AI Overviews placed above traditional results. They measured gaze patterns, recorded which results users clicked, and asked follow-up questions. The data showed increased engagement with AI content but persistent patterns from prior research—users still use traditional results substantially.

999.bp: Large language models can reason and make recommendations, but current systems rely on a single reasoning path—one train of thought that leads to a final recommendation. This is limiting because there might be multiple good ways to think about the problem, each leading to different (but valid) recommendations. Exploring multiple reasoning paths could find better and more diverse recommendations.
999.wh: When you only explore one reasoning path, you risk missing better alternatives. Imagine a recommendation system that thinks 'this user liked action movies so they'll like this thriller' but never considers 'this user also likes emotional depth, so they might prefer this drama.' Multiple different reasoning chains could reach different but valuable conclusions.
999.po: By exploring multiple reasoning paths and intelligently combining them, the system produces recommendations that are both more accurate (finding more recommendations users actually like) and more diverse (avoiding repetitive suggestions). The method doesn't require additional training on labeled data.
999.ww: Human reasoning works this way—we consider different angles before deciding. The insight is that large language models already have this capability built in; it's just that standard training uses one greedy path. By deliberately introducing controlled randomness during inference (not training), you can make the model explore multiple valid reasoning chains and combine the best ones.
999.ap: The system generates a diverse set of reasoning paths by introducing variations in how the model processes information (dropout applied at inference, small perturbations to internal representations). It then evaluates the quality of each path and selects the highest-quality subset. Finally, it uses reinforcement learning to decide how to weight and combine them, producing a recommendation that aggregates the best insights from multiple independent reasoning chains.

1000.bp: Generative recommendation systems work differently than traditional systems—instead of scoring and ranking items, they generate item identifiers directly, like a language model generates words. This requires solving two intertwined problems: encoding items into tokens (so the model can generate them) and training the model itself to generate good tokens. Current systems solve these separately, which causes misalignment.
1000.wh: Building a generative recommender requires first deciding how to encode items as tokens (words that the model will generate). This encoding step is usually trained only to make tokens easy to decode back into items, not with any consideration for whether those tokens will actually lead to good recommendations. So you get tokens that work okay at reconstruction but poorly for recommendation.
1000.po: The framework jointly optimizes tokenization and recommendation through a two-level approach, ensuring that item identifiers are both interpretable and aligned with the recommendation objective. Experiments show this improves recommendation quality on multiple real-world datasets by fixing the misalignment that hurts traditional approaches.
1000.ww: The key insight is that tokenization and recommendation are codependent—good tokens for recommendation aren't necessarily good for reconstruction. By optimizing both objectives together, considering how each change affects the other, the system ensures that tokens are informative (encode important item properties) and discriminative (different recommendations get meaningfully different tokens).
1000.ap: The system sets up two optimization levels: the lower level trains the recommender on tokenized sequences (producing recommendations), and the upper level optimizes the tokenizer based on both how well it reconstructs items and how well the recommendations perform. A meta-learning approach solves this bi-level problem efficiently, and 'gradient surgery' prevents conflicting signals from the two objectives from canceling each other out.

1001.bp: Educational systems need to diagnose what students understand and don't understand to provide personalized tutoring. Currently, they only track whether answers are right or wrong, missing crucial information about exactly what misconception led to a wrong answer. This limits how well the system can diagnose problems and offer targeted help.
1001.wh: Traditional cognitive diagnosis models treat each answer as simply correct or incorrect, ignoring that different wrong answers reveal different misconceptions. If a student answers 'B' instead of 'C' on a multiple-choice test, that's a richer signal than just 'wrong.'  But analyzing what each wrong answer reveals requires understanding the problem deeply—something traditional machine learning models struggle with.
1001.po: The system produces more accurate diagnoses of student knowledge and generates personalized learning plans that address specific misconceptions revealed by their choice of wrong answers, not just the fact that they answered incorrectly.
1001.ww: Large language models understand language and can analyze problems deeply. The insight is to use them to interpret what each answer choice represents (what misconception would lead to choosing it), then feed this semantic understanding into the diagnosis model alongside behavioral data. This combines the strengths of language models (understanding meaning) and behavioral modeling (predicting from patterns).
1001.ap: An LLM analyzes each quiz question and produces structured descriptions of what each answer choice reveals about student thinking. These descriptions are converted to embeddings (numerical representations of meaning). The diagnosis model then learns to fuse these semantic embeddings with the student's actual behavior (which answer they picked, how long it took), projecting both into a shared space where they can directly influence each other. Finally, an interpretable diagnosis layer produces both predictions and human-readable explanations.

1002.bp: Ranking systems learn to score items with large numbers so they can order them correctly. But extremely large scores cause a separate problem: the scores become overconfident, poorly calibrated. When a ranking system gives a relevance score of 1000 vs. 1001, that's meaningless—they're just saying 'first is better than second.' Real applications need scores you can trust to express how much better one item is.
1002.wh: ListMLE is a modern listwise ranking loss that learns to order entire sequences correctly. It works well for ranking, but as a side effect, it creates a feedback loop that keeps pushing scores to larger and larger values. Even after the model learns the correct ordering, gradients keep pushing scores higher, making them poorly calibrated.
1002.po: By controlling score inflation during training using temperature scaling and adjusting the loss to reduce asymmetric gradient contributions, the method produces ranking models with properly calibrated scores while maintaining ranking accuracy. This matters for real systems where scores need to be interpretable and trustworthy.
1002.ww: Score inflation happens because the loss function has a built-in asymmetry: certain pairs of positions always contribute gradients even after ordering is correct. By understanding this mechanism mathematically, you can design fixes that constrain how large scores can grow and balance the gradient contributions, preventing inflation without sacrificing ranking quality.
1002.ap: During training, the method applies temperature scaling—essentially dividing scores by a temperature parameter that constrains their magnitude. It also modifies the loss to reduce the gradient contributions from positions that aren't directly involved in ordering, preventing the asymmetric tail effects that drive inflation. The result is models that learn correct rankings but maintain reasonable, well-separated scores.

1003.bp: Multi-vector retrieval systems like ColBERTv2 represent each document with multiple dense vectors (one per passage chunk) rather than a single vector. This gives much better accuracy but is computationally expensive—comparing a query to millions of documents means millions of comparisons. Making this fast enough for real systems is hard.
1003.wh: GPU systems are great at massive parallelism but process too many candidates. CPU systems are smarter about which candidates to check but can't take advantage of parallel computation. The ideal system would combine both: efficiently reducing candidates like CPUs do, while exploiting GPU parallelism like GPUs do. It's not obvious how.
1003.po: The method achieves 11x faster query throughput and 7.6x lower latency than the previous best GPU approach while using the same retrieval accuracy, and is 2.3x cheaper per query than CPU-based systems. This makes multi-vector retrieval practical for production systems with millions of queries per second.
1003.ww: The key insight is that GPU parallelism and candidate filtering don't have to work against each other. By restructuring the candidate generation process to maintain the efficiency of filtering while exposing more parallelism, and by carefully orchestrating batches to minimize synchronization overhead, you get both benefits—fast filtering and fast computation.
1003.ap: The system implements a candidate generation kernel optimized for GPUs that preserves the effective filtering strategy of CPU systems. It then adds a score reordering mechanism that reduces the need for expensive synchronization between GPU threads, and a batching strategy that feeds queries and candidates through in batches that fit GPU memory and processing capability.

1004.bp: Knowledge base question answering answers questions using structured facts (like Freebase or Wikipedia's knowledge graph). A question like 'Who directed movies with Tom Hanks?' requires understanding the structure of the knowledge graph and finding the right path through it. Modern large language models can help, but generating correct complex structures is hard.
1004.wh: Large language models are good at understanding language but generate errors when building complex logical forms (the formal queries that specify graph structures). A single error early in the query structure breaks everything downstream—if you incorrectly identify which 'Tom' the question refers to, the whole path is wrong. Sequential generation is fragile.
1004.po: By breaking down logical form generation into steps (hop by hop), using knowledge graph facts to correct errors as they accumulate, and then assembling the paths, the system generates executable queries that work on the knowledge base at scale, dramatically reducing non-executability (queries that crash).
1004.wh: The core insight is that errors propagate. Rather than trying to generate a perfect logical form in one shot, you can generate one hop at a time, check whether it makes sense against the knowledge graph, fix it if needed, then continue. This converts a hard global problem into many easier local problems.
1004.ap: The method decomposes the question into steps, generating one hop of the logical form at a time using a fine-tuned language model. After each step, it checks the intermediate result against the knowledge graph to make sure it's executable and makes sense. If it finds issues, it uses knowledge graph facts as hints to calibrate and correct the model's next generation. Finally, it assembles the corrected hop-wise forms into a complete query.
